rubric.why: Shows that anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones.
rubric.description: States that anabolism forms complex molecules from simpler molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the build-up from simpler to more complex substances.

rubric.why: Anabolic reactions require energy.
rubric.description: States that energy is used in the process.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning energy is required or used.

modelAnswer: Anabolism is the building-up phase of metabolism in which simpler molecules are used to form more complex molecules.
It requires energy.

items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme's active site changes when a substrate binds.

rubric.why: The induced-fit model proposes that the active site is flexible rather than a rigid, exact fit before binding.
rubric.description: States that substrate binding causes the enzyme's active site to change shape.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a shape or conformational change in the active site.

rubric.why: The change allows the substrate to fit and form the enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.description: Explains that the changed active site fits the substrate, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the induced fit to substrate binding or complex formation.

modelAnswer: According to the induced-fit model, an enzyme's active site is flexible and is not an exact fit for the substrate before binding.
When the substrate binds, it induces a change in the shape of the active site so that the substrate fits and an enzyme-substrate complex forms.

rubric.why: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-carbon double bonds.
rubric.description: States that the carbon chain contains only single bonds between carbon atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the absence of carbon-carbon double bonds.

rubric.why: With no carbon-carbon double bonds, the chain carries the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms.
rubric.description: States that the fatty acid holds the maximum number of hydrogen atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the meaning of saturation in terms of hydrogen.

modelAnswer: Saturated fatty acids have carbon chains in which all carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds.
They carry the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms.

items.followUp: State two roles of red blood cells.

rubric.why: Platelets are essential for forming a blood clot.
rubric.description: States that platelets help blood to clot.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying blood clotting or coagulation as their function.

rubric.why: Clot formation helps prevent excessive blood loss from an injured blood vessel.
rubric.description: Links clotting by platelets with stopping bleeding or preventing blood loss.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the protective result of clotting.

modelAnswer: Platelets help the blood to clot at the site of an injury.
The clot seals the damaged blood vessel and helps prevent blood loss.

items.followUp: Define tissue level and give an example of an organ system.

rubric.why: An organ is formed from different tissues working together for a particular function.
rubric.description: Defines the organ level of organization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing different tissues combining to perform a specific function.

rubric.why: An organ system consists of multiple organs working together.
rubric.description: Defines the organ-system level of organization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a group of organs working together.

rubric.why: An example makes the organ-system explanation specific.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of an organ system and its organs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct system with relevant organs.

rubric.why: The organs of a system cooperate to carry out a major body function.
rubric.description: Explains what the organs in an organ system do together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the organs cooperate in carrying out a body function.

modelAnswer: Organ level: Different tissues combine and work together to perform a specific function, forming an organ.
Organ-system level: A group of organs that work together to perform a major function of the body forms an organ system.
For example, the digestive system includes organs such as the stomach and intestines.
These organs work together to digest food and absorb nutrients.

items.followUp: Draw and label a plant cell, and state two functions of its nucleus.

rubric.why: The nucleus controls and coordinates cellular activities.
rubric.description: States the controlling role of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying control or regulation of cell activities.

rubric.why: The nucleus contains the cell's genetic material.
rubric.description: States that the nucleus contains hereditary material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying genetic information, genes, or chromosomes.

rubric.why: The nucleus is enclosed by a nuclear envelope with pores.
rubric.description: Describes the nuclear envelope and its pores.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the double membrane or envelope with pores.

rubric.why: These are important internal structures shown in a standard nucleus diagram.
rubric.description: Identifies internal nuclear components.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming at least two internal components.

rubric.why: The diagram should clearly identify the boundary of the nucleus.
rubric.description: Provides a labelled nucleus diagram showing its boundary and internal structures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear labelled diagram that includes the nuclear boundary and relevant internal components such as pores, nucleoplasm, nucleolus, or chromatin.

modelAnswer: The nucleus is a prominent cell organelle that controls and coordinates the activities of the cell.
It contains hereditary material (DNA), which carries information for the cell's characteristics and activities.
The nucleus is enclosed by a double nuclear membrane, also called the nuclear envelope, which has pores.
The interior contains nucleoplasm, a nucleolus, and chromatin; chromatin condenses to form chromosomes during cell division.

Diagram: Draw a roughly circular nucleus with a double outline. Add small gaps or dots on the outline for nuclear pores. Inside, show and label nucleoplasm, a nucleolus, and threads of chromatin. Label the double outline nuclear envelope.

items.followUp: State three ways biodiversity benefits humans and ecosystems.

rubric.why: Biodiversity refers to the variety of life.
rubric.description: Defines biodiversity as the variety of living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Different organisms interact to maintain balanced and stable ecosystems.
rubric.description: Identifies the role of biodiversity in ecological balance or stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this ecological importance.

rubric.why: Biodiversity supplies useful resources to people.
rubric.description: Gives examples of useful products obtained from biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning at least one valid resource, such as food, medicines, or raw materials.

rubric.why: Biodiversity supports essential ecosystem services and useful genetic resources.
rubric.description: Gives another valid ecological or human benefit of biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another valid benefit, such as pollination, nutrient cycling, or genetic resources.

modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms found in an area or on Earth.
It helps maintain ecological balance and stable ecosystems.
It provides useful resources such as food, medicines, and raw materials.
It also supports important services such as pollination and nutrient cycling.

items.followUp: Describe the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: The dark reactions take place in the stroma of chloroplasts.
rubric.description: Identifies the site of the dark reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they occur in the chloroplast stroma.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is fixed by combining with the five-carbon acceptor RuBP.
rubric.description: Describes the initial fixation of carbon dioxide onto RuBP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying carbon dioxide and RuBP as reactants in fixation.

rubric.why: The unstable six-carbon product breaks down into molecules of PGA.
rubric.description: Names PGA as the first stable product of carbon fixation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying PGA (phosphoglycerate) as the product.

rubric.why: ATP and NADPH from the light reactions provide energy and reducing power to convert PGA to PGAL.
rubric.description: Explains the reduction of PGA to PGAL using products of the light reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking ATP and NADPH (or reduced NADP) with the conversion to PGAL.

rubric.why: Some PGAL is used to form carbohydrates, while the remainder regenerates the carbon dioxide acceptor.
rubric.description: Describes the fates of PGAL, including carbohydrate formation and regeneration of RuBP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that PGAL contributes to glucose formation and that remaining material regenerates RuBP.

modelAnswer: The dark reactions, also called the Calvin cycle, take place in the stroma of the chloroplast and do not directly require light.
Carbon dioxide combines with the five-carbon compound ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP), forming an unstable six-carbon compound.
The unstable compound immediately splits into molecules of phosphoglycerate (PGA), a three-carbon compound.
Using ATP and NADPH produced in the light reactions, PGA is reduced to phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL).
Some PGAL is used to form glucose and other carbohydrates; the remaining PGAL is used, with energy from ATP, to regenerate RuBP.
